Question: A 55-year-old male with Type 2 Diabetes (T2DM) on Dapagliflozin is scheduled for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy tomorrow morning. He has been fasting since midnight. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.name: Take half the dose on the morning of surgery.

description:
Dapagliflozin is an SGLT2 inhibitor, a class of medication associated with a risk of euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (eDKA) during the perioperative period.

Because the metabolic stress of surgery and fasting increases this risk, the FDA and various surgical guidelines recommend stopping SGLT2 inhibitors well in advance.

  • Standard protocol: Stop SGLT2 inhibitors (Dapagliflozin, Canagliflozin, Empagliflozin) 3 to 4 days before any major or scheduled surgery to allow the drug to be cleared from the system and normalize the metabolic state.
  • Risk reduction: This extended window prevents the accumulation of ketones and reduces the chance of developing ketoacidosis with relatively "normal" blood glucose levels.

Question: Which of the following mechanisms explains why SGLT2 inhibitors increase the risk of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) while maintaining normal blood glucose?

options.name: Increased glucagon-to-insulin ratio and increased ketone reabsorption in the kidney.
Inhibition of insulin production in the pancreas.
Rapid hypoglycemia causing a counter-regulatory stress response.

description:
• Increased Glucagon-to-Insulin Ratio: SGLT2 inhibitors lower blood glucose by promoting glucose excretion in the urine. This reduction in blood glucose leads to a decrease in insulin secretion from pancreatic beta-cells. Simultaneously, these drugs have been shown to directly or indirectly stimulate the release of glucagon from alpha-cells. This high glucagon/insulin ratio shifts the body into a "fasting-like" state, promoting lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis.
  • Increased Ketone Reabsorption: SGLT2 inhibitors also facilitate the secondary reabsorption of ketone bodies in the renal tubules, which raises the circulating levels of ketones in the blood even further.
  • Normal Blood Glucose (Euglycemia): Because the primary action of the drug is to dump glucose into the urine, the blood sugar levels remain relatively normal (often <250 mg/dL) despite the severe metabolic acidosis and ketosis. This is known as euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA) .

Question: A patient on Empagliflozin has a very low eGFR (<30 ml/kg/hr) preoperatively. What is the main anesthetic implication?

options.name: The drug will be more effective at reducing glucose.
The drug is less effective at causing glycosuria and risks accumulation.

description:
• Reduced Efficacy: Empagliflozin (a Sodium-Glucose Co-Transporter 2 or SGLT2 inhibitor) works by blocking glucose reabsorption in the renal proximal tubules. Its ability to lower blood glucose depends directly on the amount of glucose filtered by the kidneys, which is severely limited when the glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is low (<30 mL/min/1.73m²).
  • Risk of Accumulation: While the drug's glucose-lowering effect decreases with falling renal function, the drug itself or its metabolites can still accumulate in the body if renal clearance is impaired, potentially increasing the risk of non-glycemic side effects.

Question: 45-year-old obese patient with type 2 diabetes on weekly semaglutide (Ozempic) is scheduled for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 7 days. She took her last dose 2 days ago. What is the best course of action regarding her medication?

options.name: Cancel the surgery and reschedule in 24 hours.
Hold the medication for 7 days before surgery.
Switch to insulin for the week prior to surgery.

description:
• Hold the medication for 7 days before surgery: For weekly dosing, holding the medication for 7 days before surgery is the standard recommendation to mitigate risks of delayed gastric emptying and subsequent pulmonary aspiration under general anesthesia.
  • Proceed as scheduled: Proceeding as scheduled without holding the medication increases the risk of residual gastric contents, which could lead to life-threatening aspiration during induction.
  • Reschedule in 24 hours: Rescheduling in 24 hours is insufficient; the half-life of Ozempic is approximately one week, meaning the drug remains active in the system for several days.
  • Switch to insulin: While bridging therapy may be necessary for some diabetic patients, switching to insulin is not the primary recommendation for the week prior; rather, the ASA suggests consulting an endocrinologist for specific glucose management if GLP-1 agonists are held.

Question: A patient on daily Liraglutide presents for urgent surgery. They took their medication 4 hours ago. What is the primary anesthesia concern?

options.name: Increased risk of aspiration due to delayed gastric emptying.

description:
• Mechanism of Action: Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist. A primary side effect of this class of medication is delayed gastric emptying.
  • Anesthesia Concern: Because the patient took the medication only 4 hours ago, there is a significant risk that their stomach contains residual food or liquid even if they have followed standard fasting guidelines. This increases the risk of pulmonary aspiration during the induction of general anesthesia or deep sedation.
  • Clinical Management: For urgent surgery where the medication cannot be held, anesthesiologists often use a rapid sequence induction (RSI) or point-of-care gastric ultrasound to mitigate this risk.

Question: During anesthesia for a patient taking GLP-1 agonists, if the patient has not fasted for the appropriate time, which action is recommended?
description:
According to the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Consensus-Based Guidance, GLP-1 receptor agonists (such as Ozempic or Mounjaro) cause delayed gastric emptying, which increases the risk of pulmonary aspiration during anesthesia.

If a patient has not followed the recommended fasting or medication-holding instructions (typically holding weekly doses for 7 days or daily doses on the day of surgery), the ASA suggests that they should be treated as having a "full stomach" .

In such cases, if the surgery must proceed, a Rapid Sequence Induction is the preferred technique to secure the airway quickly and minimize the risk of aspiration.

Question: When using general anesthesia, which of the following is a key requirement for patients on long-acting GLP-1 agonists?

options.name: Routine use of a laryngeal mask airway (LMA).
Strict NPO (nothing by mouth) for only 2 hours

description:
• Symptom Assessment: If a patient has not held their GLP-1 medication as recommended, or if they are in the "escalation phase" (early treatment), clinicians must evaluate for active GI symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, bloating, or abdominal pain.
  • Risk Mitigation: The presence of these symptoms indicates a high likelihood of "full stomach" status. In such cases, the ASA recommends delaying elective surgery or using advanced precautions like point-of-care gastric ultrasound to check for retained food.

Question: 45-year-old morbidly obese female (BMI 42) is scheduled for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She takes weekly subcutaneous semaglutide (Ozempic) for diabetes, with her last dose 2 days ago. She has followed standard NPO guidelines. Which of the following is the most appropriate perioperative management?

options.name: Postpone surgery for 5 days due to high risk of aspiration.
Perform ultrasound gastric assessment; if full, proceed with caution.
Administer prokinetics and proceed with standard induction.

Question: A patient in shock is receiving an intravenous infusion of epinephrine. Which of the following, acting on beta 1-adrenergic receptors, describes a primary cardiovascular effect?

A 60-year-old female presents to the emergency department after intentionally ingesting a large amount of propranolol. She is bradycardic (35bpm) and hypotensive (80/50mm of Hg), unresponsive to atropine and fluids. Which agent is most likely to reverse these symptoms by increasing intracellular cAMP in cardiomyocytes?
description:
• Mechanism of Glucagon: Glucagon acts as a specific antidote by binding to its own G-protein-coupled receptors on cardiomyocytes.
  • Bypassing Beta-Blockade: This binding activates the enzyme adenylate cyclase through a pathway that completely bypasses the blocked beta-adrenergic receptors.
  • Intracellular Effect: Activation of adenylate cyclase leads to an increase in intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) .
  • Clinical Result: The rise in cAMP increases calcium influx, resulting in positive inotropic (increased contractility) and chronotropic (increased heart rate) effects to reverse bradycardia and hypotension.

Question: A 65-year-old female with a history of heart failure, currently taking amiodarone and furosemide, presents to the emergency department with dizziness. Her ECG shows a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (TdP) with a QTc of 580 ms. She is conscious and hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.name: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV bolus over 15 minutes

description:
The most appropriate next step for a conscious, hemodynamically stable patient with Torsades de Pointes (TdP) and a prolonged QTc is intravenous Magnesium sulfate.

The recommended dose is 2 g IV, which can be repeated if the arrhythmia persists. Magnesium is the first-line treatment for suppressing early afterdepolarizations and terminating TdP.

Question: A 50-year-old male with acute diarrhea and hypokalemia develops recurrent episodes of TdP. He has already received 4 g of magnesium sulfate, but the rhythm persists. What is the next best action?
description:
In a patient with refractory Torsades de Pointes (TdP) who has already failed to respond to initial high-dose magnesium (4 g), the standard next-line therapy is to increase the heart rate to shorten the QT interval.

  • Mechanism: Increasing the heart rate via overdrive pacing (typically at 100–120 bpm) effectively shortens the ventricular repolarisation period (QT interval). This eliminates the "pauses" (short-long-short sequences) that typically trigger TdP.
  • Efficacy: It is considered the treatment of choice for refractory or recurrent TdP when magnesium and electrolyte correction are insufficient.
  • Alternatives: If pacing is not immediately available, a chronotropic drug like isoproterenol can be used as a bridge, provided the patient does not have congenital long QT syndrome.

Question: A 70-year-old patient with end-stage renal disease and a prolonged QTc develops TdP. Which of the following is true regarding magnesium administration?

options.name: Magnesium should be avoided due to the high risk of immediate hypermagnesemia.
A lower dose should be used, with frequent monitoring of magnesium levels and deep tendon reflexes.
Calcium gluconate must be given before magnesium.

description:
• Life-Saving Intervention: Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the first-line treatment for terminating Torsades de Pointes (TdP), even in patients with normal magnesium levels, as it stabilizes the cardiac membrane by blocking L-type calcium channels.
  • Renal Impairment Risks: In patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) , the kidneys cannot effectively excrete magnesium, leading to a significantly higher risk of hypermagnesemia and toxicity.
  • Standard Protocol: To balance the urgent need to treat a life-threatening arrhythmia against the risk of toxicity, clinical guidelines recommend a reduced dosage in renal impairment, coupled with rigorous monitoring of serum levels and clinical signs like deep tendon reflexes (loss of these reflexes is an early sign of magnesium toxicity).

Question: Following the administration of 2 g of Magnesium Sulfate, the TdP in a patient with LQTS resolves. However, a repeat ECG 10 minutes later shows that the QTc interval remains at 600 ms. What is the best interpretation?

options.name: Magnesium works by directly inhibiting early afterdepolarizations (EADs) rather than immediately shortening the QT interval.
The patient is at risk of imminent recurrence

description:
Magnesium sulfate is the first-line treatment for Torsades de Pointes (TdP) in both acquired and congenital Long QT Syndrome (LQTS).

Its primary mechanism of action in this context is to stabilize the cardiac membrane by inhibiting early afterdepolarizations (EADs) , which are the fundamental triggers for TdP.

Crucially, magnesium terminates and prevents the arrhythmia without necessarily shortening the QTc interval. Therefore, a persistent QTc of 600 ms after the resolution of the arrhythmia is an expected finding and does not indicate treatment failure.

Question: A 65-year-old male presents to the ER with chest pain and ECG shows wide-complex tachycardia (Ventricular Tachycardia). He is stable, but a history of acute myocardial infarction is confirmed. Which of the following is the drug of choice for immediate management?
description:
• Mechanism: Lignocaine is a Class Ib antiarrhythmic that blocks sodium channels, particularly in ischemic or depolarized myocardial tissue.
  • Suitability: It is highly effective for suppressing ventricular arrhythmias arising from an ischemic substrate, such as a prior or acute MI.

Question: During a cardiac arrest scenario, a patient is in shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation (VF). Amiodarone is not available. According to ACLS guidelines, what is the next best pharmacological option?

A patient with acute myocardial infarction is receiving an IV infusion of lidocaine for recurrent VT. The patient complains of lightheadedness, numbness around the mouth and becomes drowsy. What is the most likely cause?
description:
The patient is exhibiting classic neurological signs of lidocaine toxicity, often referred to by the acronym SAMS (Slurred speech, Altered central nervous system, Muscle twitching, and Seizures).

Lidocaine is a sodium channel blocker that, when reaching toxic levels, primarily affects the central nervous system before causing cardiovascular collapse.

  • Specific symptoms mentioned align with early-to-moderate lidocaine toxicity:
  • Lightheadedness and Drowsiness: Early CNS depressive effects as the drug crosses the blood-brain barrier.
  • Numbness around the mouth (Paresthesia): Circumoral numbness is a hallmark early warning sign of local anesthetic systemic toxicity.

Question: How does lidocaine act as an antiarrhythmic agent?

options.name: Blocks fast sodium channels and shortens action potential duration

description:
Lidocaine acts as a Class Ib antiarrhythmic agent by binding to and blocking fast sodium channels in the inactivated state, primarily in ischemic or depolarized ventricular tissue, which reduces action potential duration.

It is particularly effective at treating ventricular tachyarrhythmias (VT/VF) by reducing abnormal automaticity.

Question: During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the monitor shows a wide-complex rhythm at a rate of 150 bpm. The pulse is palpable, and the BP is stable. What is the most appropriate pharmacological intervention?
description:
• Amiodarone or Procainamide: These are the first-line pharmacological treatments for hemodynamically stable wide-complex tachycardia. Amiodarone is typically administered as a 150 mg IV dose over 10 minutes. Procainamide is also a first-choice drug for stable patients, especially if Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is suspected.
  • Verapamil and Digoxin: These agents are contraindicated in wide-complex tachycardia of unknown origin because they can cause severe hemodynamic collapse and even degenerate the rhythm into ventricular fibrillation if the rhythm is actually ventricular tachycardia or pre-excited SVT.
  • Adenosine: While adenosine can be considered for monomorphic regular wide-complex tachycardia (to rule out SVT with aberrancy), it is generally avoided in irregular or polymorphic rhythms and is not the definitive first-line pharmacological choice for undifferentiated stable wide-complex tachycardia compared to antiarrhythmics like Amiodarone.
